extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers or students interested in philosophy, education, and the scientific outlook
extracted.subtask_description: Expository essay articulating standards for what education should aim to produce, the virtues of a scientific outlook, and moral/aesthetic responses appropriate to a scientifically informed view of the world. Covers intellectual habits, aims of instruction, scientific temper, and the ethical/spiritual stance of the 'free man'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of education (formation of mental habits and outlook)
rubrics_metrics.description: Education, in the sense used here, is 'the formation, by means of instruction, of certain mental habits and a certain outlook on life and the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success of education is to be judged by what mental habits and what sort of outlook it produces. Distinguish this sense from the broader 'education of life' and the narrower sense of mere instruction (reading, writing, arithmetic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlarge scope of primary impulses (not replace nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of education cannot be to create any primary impulse lacking in the uneducated; it can only 'enlarge the scope of those that human nature provides, by increasing the number and variety of attendant thoughts, and by showing where the most permanent satisfaction is to be found.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid educational approaches that seek to 'thwart or eradicate nature' (e.g., produce hypocrites by suppressing natural impulses); instead cultivate and broaden natural desires so they connect to more permanent satisfactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destroy crudity of instinct / cultivate civic/universal outlook
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should 'destroy the crudity of instinct, and increase through knowledge the wealth and variety of the individual's contacts with the outside world,' making him 'a citizen of the universe' whose interests embrace distant countries and vast stretches of past and future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate curricula and pedagogy by their capacity to soften narrow insistence of desire and to enlarge intellectual and moral horizons beyond immediate impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form an objective view of the world
rubrics_metrics.description: A chief intellectual aim of education is 'to make us see and imagine the world in an objective manner, as far as possible as it is in itself, and not merely through the distorting medium of personal desire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure educational outcomes by approximation to this ideal: ability to recognize one's biases, to perceive social and non-human reality apart from personal wants, and to form judgments based on evidence rather than appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education judged by approximation to objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Education, considered as forming mental habits and outlook, is 'to be judged successful in proportion as its outcome approximates' the ideal of objective perception and correct understanding of our place in society and the non-human world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this standard when comparing methods (e.g., science vs. classical study): prefer those that better cultivate objective judgment and accurate understanding of relations between society and environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific education fosters hopefulness and cumulative progress
rubrics_metrics.description: One merit of science is 'hopefulness as to the future of human achievement' because scientific method produces cumulative progress: 'where one man of supreme genius has invented a method, a thousand lesser men can apply it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess disciplines or pedagogies by whether they offer practical pathways for many students to contribute, and whether they foster belief in continuing, cumulative improvement rather than reliance on solitary genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method's kernel: refuse subjective desires as keys
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'kernel of the scientific outlook is the refusal to regard our own desires, tastes, and interests as affording a key to the understanding of the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, this requires suppression of hopes, fears, loves and hates when evaluating evidence; avoid drawing factual conclusions from æsthetico-moral preferences (Aristotle's circular or Malthusian examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value scientific temper over particular scientific conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The temper and method of inquiry (the scientific spirit) are of higher value than any specific conclusions; a method treating man 'as a part of nature' remains valuable even if particular inferences (e.g., Malthus) are erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging theories or arguments, prioritize whether the approach is disinterested, empirically grounded and methodical, rather than whether initial conclusions match current belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should adopt an ethically neutral/scientific attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy largely lacks the scientific spirit; to make progress it must learn to think of the universe 'in ethically neutral terms' and avoid conceiving the universe to mirror human mind or moral hopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate philosophical positions by whether they avoid anthropocentric projection and maintain impartial inquiry rather than conforming cosmology to human desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about scientific truths as basis for ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Given scientific truths about man's accidental origins and the universe's indifference, 'only within the scaffolding of these truths... can the soul's habitation henceforward be safely built.' Ideals should be formed honestly on the recognition of these facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral or religious projects by whether they confront, rather than deny, the scientific picture of human contingency, constructing values that accept rather than evade despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject worship of Power; prioritize worship of Goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'worship Force' (Carlyle/Nietzsche/Militarism); rather 'worship only the God created by our own love of the good'—respect ideals of truth, beauty and goodness even if the universe is indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical evaluation should reject valorizing brute power and instead esteem moral strength that defends ideals contrary to mere factual power; beware conflating 'fitness' or power with moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom as submission of desires and liberty of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: True freedom is 'the submission of our desires, but not of our thoughts' — Stoic-style restraint of appetites combined with intellectual independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish justified resignation (courageously bearing inevitable loss) from bitter indignation; judge character by capacity to restrain impulsive desire while retaining critical, imaginative thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renunciation and the gate of wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Renunciation—learning that the world was not made for us and bearing misfortune without repining—is 'the very gate of wisdom'; the young must learn the 'great renunciation' that comes with life's limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational or moral programs should cultivate courage and acceptance alongside striving; evaluate maturity by capacity to accept unattainable goods without resentful longing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art/Tragedy as mastery over Fate and source of insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy and high art 'build[] its shining citadel in the very centre of the enemy's country' — they transmute suffering into insight and beauty, enabling reconquest of the world by the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge aesthetic works by their capacity to incorporate suffering and mortality into a vision that dignifies human experience, rather than by mere escapism or nihilistic rebellion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity and sympathy as ethical duty under common doom
rubrics_metrics.description: United by 'the tie of a common doom,' the free man should 'shed sunshine on [others'] path, to lighten their sorrows by the balm of sympathy... to strengthen failing courage,' judging others by need rather than grudging merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluation of conduct should emphasize responsiveness to fellow-sufferers' needs; educational aims include fostering sympathy and readiness to assist, not cold merit-counting.
